edges.description: Because EFNB1 is subject to X-inactivation, a heterozygous loss-of-function variant leaves a female with a mosaic of ephrin-B1-positive and ephrin-B1-deficient cells. A post-zygotic variant does the same in a male.
Independently of mosaicism, loss of ephrin-B1 acts autonomously in neural crest cells and disturbs their migration, the defect shared by hemizygous males and heterozygous females.
edges.target: Impaired Cranial Neural Crest Cell Migration

edges.description: Diaphragmatic hernia occurs in hemizygous males with only minor craniofacial features, so it is attributed to ephrin-B1 deficiency itself rather than to mosaicism. The developmental step involved is not known.
Ephrin-B1-positive and ephrin-B1-negative cells sort apart, so new Eph/ephrin interfaces form where none should exist.

nodes.description: A grooved or bifid nasal tip, with columellar indentation.

evidence.reference_title: Phenotypes of craniofrontonasal syndrome in patients with a pathogenic mutation in EFNB1.
evidence.snippet: Frequently observed phenotypic features were bifid tip of the nose (91%), columellar indentation (91%) and low implantation of breasts (90%).

nodes.description: Induced pluripotent stem cells from heterozygous female patients differentiated to neuroepithelial cells.
Cleft palate, usually together with cleft lip, is a less frequent feature.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia: a surgical treatment algorithm.
evidence.snippet: Patients also had cleft lip-cleft palate (10 percent)

nodes.description: Diaphragmatic hernia, reported in hemizygous boys with otherwise minimal craniofacial findings as well as in females.

evidence.reference_title: Expanding the phenotype of craniofrontonasal syndrome: two unrelated boys with EFNB1 mutations and congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
evidence.snippet: although the sons have no major craniofacial features other than telecanthus, both had a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)

nodes.description: Efnb1 marks the position of the future coronal suture, the boundary between neural crest-derived frontal bone and mesoderm-derived parietal bone. Patchwork ephrin-B1 loss is proposed to disturb this boundary in heterozygous females; hemizygous males, who lack the patchwork, rarely have craniosynostosis.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), a marker of tissue boundary formation, cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: In mice, the orthologous Efnb1 gene is expressed in the frontonasal neural crest and demarcates the position of the future coronal suture.

nodes.description: Unilateral or bilateral coronal synostosis in females, giving plagiocephaly or brachycephaly respectively. It is uncommon in hemizygous males.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), a marker of tissue boundary formation, cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Females have frontonasal dysplasia and coronal craniosynostosis (fusion of the coronal sutures)

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia: a surgical treatment algorithm.
evidence.snippet: Eight patients had unilateral coronal synostosis (plagiocephaly) and 13 had bilateral coronal synostosis (brachycephaly).

nodes.description: Abnormal shaping of the neural crest-derived frontonasal and midfacial primordia produces frontonasal dysplasia: widely spaced orbits, a broad or grooved nasal tip and facial asymmetry. Hemizygous and heterozygous mouse embryos show qualitatively similar face-shape changes, more severe in heterozygotes, matching the human sex difference.

evidence.reference_title: Aberrant cell segregation in the craniofacial primordium and the emergence of facial dysmorphology in craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Whereas specific craniofacial shape changes are qualitatively similar in Efnb1 heterozygous and hemizygous mutant embryos, heterozygous embryos are quantitatively more severely affected

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of the ephrin-B1 gene cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: In all cases, mutations were found consistently in obligate male carriers, clinically affected males, and affected heterozygous females. We conclude that mutations in EFNB1 cause CFNS.

evidence.reference_title: Twenty-six novel EFNB1 mutations in familial and sporadic craniofrontonasal syndrome (CFNS).
evidence.snippet: DNA sequencing revealed mutations in 33 (86.8%) cases including 26 distinct novel mutations.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal syndrome in a patient with an inv(X)(p22.2q13.1), separating EFNB1 from its enhancer.
evidence.snippet: One of the breakpoints was about 97 kbp downstream of the 3' end of the EFNB1 gene, separating a potential EFNB1 enhancer region from the EFNB1 gene.

evidence.reference_title: Cellular interference in craniofrontonasal syndrome: males mosaic for mutations in the X-linked EFNB1 gene are more severely affected than true hemizygotes.
evidence.snippet: The 5' UTR variant mutates the stop codon of a small upstream open reading frame that, using a dual-luciferase reporter construct, was demonstrated to exacerbate interference with translation of the wild-type protein.

nodes.description: Heterozygous (female), hemizygous (male) or mosaic loss-of-function variants in EFNB1 - nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, missense variants in the extracellular ephrin domain, and whole-gene deletions - abolish ephrin-B1 function. Missense variants cluster in the receptor-binding and oligomerization surfaces, and C-terminal frameshifts remove the intracellular PDZ and Grb4 binding sites needed for reverse signaling.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), a marker of tissue boundary formation, cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: the classical female CFNS phenotype is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in EFNB1, which encodes a member of the ephrin family of transmembrane ligands for Eph receptor tyrosine kinases

evidence.reference_title: Twenty-six novel EFNB1 mutations in familial and sporadic craniofrontonasal syndrome (CFNS).
evidence.snippet: We conclude that the major causes of familial as well as sporadic CFNS are loss of function mutations in the EFNB1 gene that comprise premature termination or abrogate receptor-ligand interaction, oligomerization, and ephrin-B1 reverse signaling.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of the ephrin-B1 gene cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Both mutations are located in multimerization and receptor-interaction motifs found within the ephrin-B1 extracellular domain.

nodes.description: Mosaic ephrin-B1 expression drives segregation of expressing and non-expressing cells, first in the early neuroepithelium and later in craniofacial mesenchyme. Sorting is driven by unidirectional EphB kinase signaling into ephrin-B1-expressing neighbors, which creates a Rho kinase-dependent cortical actomyosin differential. EPHB2 and EPHB3 are the main receptors in craniofacial tissue. The ectopic boundaries are the proposed basis of cellular interference.
nodes.id: Ectopic Eph-Ephrin Boundaries and Cell Segregation

animal_models.description: X-inactivation mosaicism in heterozygous females drives ephrin-B1 cell segregation, as proposed in CFNS.
animal_models.name: Efnb1 heterozygous and hemizygous mice

biological_processes: ephrin receptor signaling pathway (ectopic, at mosaic interfaces)

evidence.reference_title: Unidirectional Eph/ephrin signaling creates a cortical actomyosin differential to drive cell segregation.
evidence.snippet: unidirectional EphB kinase signaling leads to cell sorting by the Rho kinase-dependent generation of a cortical actin differential between ephrin-B1- and EphB-expressing cells

evidence.reference_title: Aberrant cell segregation in the craniofacial primordium and the emergence of facial dysmorphology in craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: EPHRIN-B1 regulates cell segregation independently in early neural development and later in craniofacial development, correlating with the emergence of quantitative differences in face shape

evidence.reference_title: Aberrant cell segregation in the craniofacial primordium and the emergence of facial dysmorphology in craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: EPHB2 and EPHB3 play an important role in craniofacial cell segregation, EPHB1 is more important for cell segregation in the brain

experimental_models.description: Mosaic neuroepithelial cultures segregate into ephrin-B1-positive and -negative domains.
experimental_models.name: CFNS patient-derived hiPSC neuroepithelial cells

nodes.description: Efnb1 null mice die perinatally with skeletal patterning defects; heterozygous females, mosaic through X-inactivation, show cell sorting and phenotypes absent from null males, such as preaxial polydactyly.

Random X-inactivation in heterozygous females (or a post-zygotic variant in males) produces intermingled populations of ephrin-B1-expressing and ephrin-B1-deficient cells. A uniformly deficient hemizygous male lacks this mosaic, which is why he is usually mildly affected. Mosaicism for two different expression levels, as with an EFNB1 duplication or a supernumerary X carrying EFNB1, has a similar effect.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), a marker of tissue boundary formation, cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Although EFNB1 is X-inactivated, we did not observe markedly skewed X-inactivation in either blood or cranial periosteum from females with CFNS, indicating that lack of ephrin-B1 does not compromise cell viability in these tissues.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal syndrome in a male due to chromosomal mosaicism involving EFNB1: further insights into a genetic paradox.
evidence.snippet: Mosaicism for cell populations with different levels of EFNB1 expression can explain the severe phenotype of this patient.

evidence.reference_title: Duplication of the EFNB1 gene in familial hypertelorism: imbalance in ephrin-B1 expression and abnormal phenotypes in humans and mice.
evidence.snippet: cellular mosaicism for different levels of ephrin-B1 (as well as simple presence/absence) leads to craniofacial abnormalities

experimental_models.description: Patient lines retain X-inactivation mosaicism for ephrin-B1.
experimental_models.name: CFNS patient-derived hiPSC neuroepithelial cells

nodes.description: Craniofacial asymmetry, often with asymmetric hypertelorism.

evidence.reference_title: Cellular interference in craniofrontonasal syndrome: males mosaic for mutations in the X-linked EFNB1 gene are more severely affected than true hemizygotes.
evidence.snippet: synostosis of the coronal sutures (unilateral or bilateral), craniofacial asymmetry, downslanting palpebral fissures, fine frizzy hair

nodes.description: Fronto-orbital advancement for coronal synostosis in infancy. In a 21-patient series no patient had raised intracranial pressure or resynostosis afterwards.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia: a surgical treatment algorithm.
evidence.snippet: After fronto-orbital advancement, no patients had increased intracranial pressure problems or difficulty related to resynostosis.

nodes.description: Ephrin-B1 binds connexin 43 and controls its distribution. At the ectopic boundaries in ephrin-B1 mosaic tissue, gap junction communication between neighboring cells is inhibited.
nodes.id: Gap Junction Communication Block at Ectopic Boundaries

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of gap junction communication at ectopic Eph/ephrin boundaries underlies craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Our results uncover a novel role for Eph/ephrins in regulating GJC in vivo and suggest that the pleiotropic defects seen in CFNS patients are due to improper regulation of GJC in affected tissues.

nodes.description: Marked, often asymmetric, hypertelorism. It is the one feature shared by heterozygous females and hemizygous males, and is usually the only sign in males.

evidence.reference_title: Phenotypes of craniofrontonasal syndrome in patients with a pathogenic mutation in EFNB1.
evidence.snippet: Hypertelorism, longitudinal ridging and/or splitting of nails, a (mild) webbed neck and a clinodactyly of one or more toes were the only consistent features observed in all patients.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations of ephrin-B1 (EFNB1), a marker of tissue boundary formation, cause craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: in males, hypertelorism is the only typical manifestation

nodes.description: Orbital translocation by facial bipartition or box osteotomy. Early correction relapsed in some patients, so it is usually delayed until the permanent maxillary incisors have erupted.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia: a surgical treatment algorithm.
evidence.snippet: Because of this, correction in later patients was delayed until after eruption of permanent maxillary incisors.

evidence.reference_title: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia: hypertelorism correction in late presenting patients.
evidence.snippet: The absence of elevated intracranial pressure enables hypertelorism correction in late presenting CFND patients via facial bipartition or box osteotomy without the need for additional operations that provide for cranial expansion.

nodes.description: In ephrin-B1 heterozygous mice, calvarial defects arise autonomously in neural crest cells, correlate with cell sorting, and trace to impaired differentiation of osteogenic precursors. This is a mouse finding; how it relates to the coronal synostosis seen in patients is not settled.

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of gap junction communication at ectopic Eph/ephrin boundaries underlies craniofrontonasal syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Here we show that ephrin-B1(+/-) mice exhibit calvarial defects, a phenotype autonomous to neural crest cells that correlates with cell sorting. We have traced the causes of calvarial defects to impaired differentiation of osteogenic precursors.

nodes.description: Ephrin-B1 acts cell-autonomously in neural crest cells, and its PDZ-dependent reverse signaling is required there; complete loss disturbs neural crest migration and neural crest-derived tissues. The frontonasal neural crest expresses Efnb1.
nodes.id: Impaired Cranial Neural Crest Cell Migration

evidence.reference_title: Ephrin-B1 forward and reverse signaling are required during mouse development.
evidence.snippet: Last, a mutation in the PDZ binding domain indicated that ephrin-B1-induced reverse signaling is required in NCCs.

nodes.description: In the anterior palatal shelf mesenchyme, ephrin-B1 forward signaling through ERK/MAPK controls proliferation. In heterozygous mice the mosaic of expressing and non-expressing cells disrupts proliferation patchily, which correlates with the more severe palatal dysmorphogenesis of heterozygotes.
nodes.id: Mosaic Disruption of Palatal Mesenchyme Proliferation

evidence.reference_title: Ephrin-B1 forward signaling regulates craniofacial morphogenesis by controlling cell proliferation across Eph-ephrin boundaries.
evidence.snippet: we show that ephrin-B1 controls proliferation in the palate by regulating the extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase (ERK/MAPK) signal transduction pathway
